bibl.title: Masked Cross-Modal Repetition Priming: An Event-Related Potential Investigation

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: mechanism
span.quote: These results therefore confirm the first prediction derived from the bi-modal interactive-activation model, namely that lexical-level pathways dominate cross-modal transfer.

span.label: masked cross-modal repetition priming in word recognition
span.quote: In the current study we examined ERP masked repetition priming both within and between modalities.

span.label: electrophysiology
span.quote: We report three experiments that combine the masked priming paradigm with the recording of event-related potentials in order to examine the time-course of cross-modal interactions during word recognition.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: A visual prime activates whole-word orthographic representations, which pass activation on to the corresponding whole-word phonological representations, so cross-modal transfer travels the slower lexical route and shows up only in the N400.
span.quote: Activation engendered by a visual prime word reaches whole-word orthographic representations (giving rise to within-modality priming) and is sent on to corresponding whole-word phonological representations.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Lengthening prime exposure lets activation reach whole-word phonological units sooner and accumulate to a higher level, which shifts the cross-modal N400 effect earlier and makes it bigger.
span.quote: suggests that the longer prime duration allowed activation to reach whole-word phonological representations earlier and therefore to build up to higher levels than at the shorter prime duration

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: An inhibitory reset of modality-specific representations, triggered when prime and target are perceived as separate events, reduces within-modality priming at longer prime durations.
span.quote: One plausible mechanism for such inhibitory effects is that the word recognition system needs to be reset in order to correctly process new upcoming words.

span.label: The post-experiment mask-effectiveness test probably overstates how visible the primes were during the ERP experiment itself.
span.quote: Note, however, that as in Experiment 1, the mask-effectiveness test is likely to have over estimated the visibility of primes during the ERP experiment as it focused attention on detecting the masked items themselves ( Kahan, 2000 ).

span.label: The larger, earlier cross-modal effect at 67 ms may reflect removal of an early reversed priming effect rather than a genuinely larger N400; the authors cannot yet decide between these.
span.quote: One admittedly speculative possibility for the different size and time-course of priming effects across experiments is that the reversal effect in the first two experiments blocked or obscured the earlier phase of the N400 seen in Experiment 3 and that the resulting larger and somewhat earlier effect in Experiment 3 is more a reflection of the removal of the reversal than the addition of a larger/earlier N400.

span.label: That alternative explanation is untested in the present data and awaits further experiments.
span.quote: Testing of this hypothesis will have to await further experimentation.

span.label: Cross-study comparison of effect magnitude is difficult; the auditory priming effect obtained here is small and late relative to a previous cross-modal study.
span.quote: Although direct between-study comparisons are difficult to make, it is worth noting that the current 1.2 microvolt auditory priming effect at Cz between 500 and 750 ms is relatively late and somewhat small compared to at least one previous cross-modal priming study.

span.label: cross-modal priming
span.quote: whereas cross-modal priming should only be reflected in later components associated with activation at the level of whole-word representations (i.e., the N400)

span.label: within-modality priming
span.quote: Within-modality priming would be more automatic, involving the pre-activation of appropriate representations by the prime stimulus (the approach adopted within the framework of the bimodal interactive-activation model), whereas priming across modalities would reflect the operation of controlled processes involved in establishing connections across modality-specific representations

span.label: N250
span.quote: where within-modality priming revealed an early N250 effect that was absent in the cross-modality condition

span.label: N400
span.quote: On the other hand, priming effects in the region of the N400 appeared to be just as strong cross-modalities as within-modalities in this experiment

span.label: bimodal interactive-activation model
span.quote: The present results are compatible with the first prediction of the bimodal interactive-activation model, that lexical-level pathways dominate cross-modal transfer

span.label: prime duration
span.quote: However, contrary to this prediction we failed to find any evidence for standard priming effects (i.e., reduced negativity in the related condition) in early ERP components (i.e., the N250) with auditory targets at the longer prime duration of Experiment 3

span.label: THEY CONSIDER Holcomb2005'S DISTINCTION FOR THIS CASE AND DECLINE IT - AND Holcomb AND Grainger ARE AUTHORS ON BOTH PAPERS. The obvious extension of `pre-activation versus establishing connections` is that cross-modal priming, being slower and later, is the connection-building kind. `HOWEVER, WE WOULD ARGUE that while semantic priming may indeed require the conscious linking of related representations, SUCH A MECHANISM WOULD BE SUPERFLUOUS FOR CROSS-MODAL REPETITION PRIMING since the visual prime and auditory target presumably have THE SAME SEMANTIC REPRESENTATION.` The argument is that the distinction does not APPLY here, not that it is wrong - a author group declining to extend its own account into the case it most obviously fits
span.quote: However, we would argue that while semantic priming may indeed require the conscious linking of related representations, such a mechanism would be superfluous for cross-modal repetition priming since the visual prime and auditory target presumably have the same semantic representation

span.label: AND THEY BACK THE REFUSAL WITH AN EMPIRICAL DISCRIMINATOR RATHER THAN LEAVING IT AS REASONING: the Holcomb et al. (2005) semantic effect `was mainly evident on the MIDDLE PORTION AND TRAILING EDGE of the N400, while cross-modal repetition priming was evident on the RISING EDGE of the N400 at the longest prime duration of the present study.` Different position within the same component, so the two effects are not one phenomenon wearing two names. That is a much harder claim to make than a verbal distinction, and it is the kind of evidence a corpus of definitions should be able to retrieve: two papers, one lab, one component, and a measurable difference in WHERE on the waveform each effect sits
span.quote: Furthermore, the semantic priming effect that emerged with longer prime durations in the Holcomb et al. (2005) study was mainly evident on the middle portion and trailing edge of the N400, while cross-modal repetition priming was evident on the rising edge of the N400 at the longest prime duration of the present study

span.label: A METHODOLOGICAL CRITERION FOR WHETHER AN ERP COMPONENT EXISTS AT ALL, cited to a standard and RANKED BY STRENGTH: `THIRD, THE MOST COMPELLING EVIDENCE for component independence is when components show DIFFERENTIAL SENSITIVITY TO EXPERIMENTAL VARIABLES (Rugg & Coles, 1995).` The first two pieces of evidence are morphological - two peaks with a positivity between them, different scalp distributions - and the authors say plainly that the functional one beats them. **A component is real when something moves it that does not move its neighbour**, and that is a rule about how to individuate a measure, not a finding about words
span.quote: Third, the most compelling evidence for component independence is when components show differential sensitivity to experimental variables

span.label: THE PAPER'S OWN DISSOCIATION SUPPLIES THAT CRITERION, AND IT IS A DOUBLE ONE: `within-modality priming revealed an early N250 effect THAT WAS ABSENT in the cross-modality condition. On the other hand, priming effects in the region of the N400 appeared to be JUST AS STRONG cross-modalities as within-modalities in this experiment.` One variable moves the early component and not the late one; the other moves both. So the N250's null in the cross-modal condition is not a weak result - it is the evidence that the N250 is a component rather than a shoulder of the N400
span.quote: In the current series of studies such a dissociation occurred in the comparisons of within and across modality priming in Experiment 3 where within-modality priming revealed an early N250 effect that was absent in the cross-modality condition. On the other hand, priming effects in the region of the N400 appeared to be just as strong cross-modalities as within-modalities in this experiment. Together these data strongly suggest that the N250 and N400 are at least partially distinct and emanate from non-identical neural sources

span.label: THE MODEL IS TESTED ON TWO PREDICTIONS AND THE PAPER REPORTS BOTH OUTCOMES, INCLUDING THE FAILURE. The first holds - `The present results are compatible with the FIRST prediction of the bimodal interactive-activation model, that lexical-level pathways dominate cross-modal transfer.` The second does not: `HOWEVER, CONTRARY TO THIS PREDICTION WE FAILED TO FIND ANY EVIDENCE for standard priming effects ... in early ERP components (i.e., the N250) with auditory targets at the longer prime duration.` They then explain the failure within the model - the sublexical units get only one source of activation where whole-word units get two - and mark that explanation as owing a test: whether another small increase in prime duration would produce the effect `remains to be seen in further research`
span.quote: However, contrary to this prediction we failed to find any evidence for standard priming effects (i.e., reduced negativity in the related condition) in early ERP components (i.e., the N250) with auditory targets at the longer prime duration of Experiment 3

span.label: replicates → Grainger et al. (2003) behavioural cross-modal masked priming result
span.quote: Experiment 1 successfully replicated the behavioral pattern of within and cross-modality masked repetition priming obtained in prior studies using the lexical decision task and similar stimulus presentation conditions (i.e., 50 ms visual primes, Grainger et al., 2003 ).

span.label: builds-on → Holcomb and Grainger (in press), the N250 component
span.quote: In line with the results of Holcomb and Grainger (in press) , in Experiment 1 we also found evidence for visual-visual repetition effects starting as early as 200–300 ms post-target onset that resulted in a clear negative-going peak at 250 ms (see Figure 4 ).

span.label: contradicts → the second prediction of the bimodal interactive-activation model (early, pre-N400 cross-modal effects at 67 ms primes)
span.quote: However, contrary to this prediction we failed to find any evidence for standard priming effects (i.e., reduced negativity in the related condition) in early ERP components (i.e., the N250) with auditory targets at the longer prime duration of Experiment 3.

span.label: within-modality priming —contrasted-with→ cross-modal priming
span.note: differs in: BOTH THE KIND OF DIFFERENCE AND ITS SIZE - the two words are the paper's own. Qualitatively: within-modality priming moves the early N250 and cross-modal priming does not, so they engage different processing stages rather than the same stage to different degrees. Quantitatively: at 50 ms prime exposures the cross-modal N400 effect is much the weaker of the two, though at 67 ms it is not · strength of the relation: 0.9 — GROUNDED ON THE RESULT RATHER THAN ON THE INTERPRETATION, AND THAT WAS A CORRECTION. The span I first chose here - `within-modality priming WOULD BE more automatic ... whereas priming across modalities WOULD REFLECT controlled processes` - states an account the authors DECLINE two sentences later. Grounding the contrast on it would have recorded a position as this paper's when it is the one being argued against. That reasoning is in the sense rows instead, with the refusal attached to it.
span.quote: However, as with Experiment 1, the cross-modal priming effects were both qualitatively and quantitatively distinct from within-modality priming

span.label: prime duration —causes→ cross-modal priming
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.6 — the record marks this weak — WEIGHT 0.6 BECAUSE THIS IS AN OPEN QUESTION THE AUTHORS FLAG, NOT A RESULT - `it REMAINS TO BE SEEN in further research`, and the hedge is the first clause of the quote. The established half of this relation (50 ms to 67 ms made the cross-modal N400 effect earlier and larger) is already on the record as content_tags.findings[2]; what is added here is the part the paper does NOT know - whether the same dial reaches the pre-N400 components its model predicted and Experiment 3 failed to find. No effect_direction: a conditional has no measured sign (Q-777).
span.quote: Thus, it remains to be seen in further research whether another small increase in prime duration is all that is necessary to generate cross-modal priming effects in pre-N400 components

span.label: N250 —distinct-from→ N400
span.note: differs in: WHAT MOVES THEM. Within-modality priming moves the N250; cross-modality priming does not; both move the N400 equally. That is differential sensitivity to an experimental variable, which the authors name as the most compelling evidence for component independence - stronger than the two morphological arguments (two peaks with an intervening positivity, different scalp distributions) that precede it · strength of the relation: 0.9 — `at least PARTIALLY distinct` and `strongly SUGGEST` are the hedges and both are inside the quote. The claim is that two measures are two things - an unusual thing for a concept edge to carry, and the reason this record is worth its senses.
span.quote: In the current series of studies such a dissociation occurred in the comparisons of within and across modality priming in Experiment 3 where within-modality priming revealed an early N250 effect that was absent in the cross-modality condition. On the other hand, priming effects in the region of the N400 appeared to be just as strong cross-modalities as within-modalities in this experiment. Together these data strongly suggest that the N250 and N400 are at least partially distinct and emanate from non-identical neural sources

span.label: repeated measures ANOVA
span.quote: Four separate repeated measures analyses of variance (ANOVAs) were conducted using the within-subject factors of repetition (repeated vs. unrelated) and modality (visual vs. auditory)

span.label: Geisser-Greenhouse sphericity correction
span.quote: The Geisser-Greenhouse (1959) correction was applied to all repeated measures with more than one degree of freedom.

span.label: t-test
span.quote: The average d’ value was 0.11, and this did not significantly differ from zero (t(23)=1.19, p =0.24).

span.label: signal-detection sensitivity (d-prime)
span.quote: The average d’ value was 0.11, and this did not significantly differ from zero (t(23)=1.19, p =0.24).

span.label: mean and standard error of the mean
span.term: mean and standard error of the mean
span.quote: The mean reaction times, percentage of errors, and standard error of the mean were calculated for each subject.

span.label: z-score normalisation
span.quote: An ANOVA performed on both the raw ERP mean amplitudes as well as those normalized using a z-score procedure (Holcomb et al., 1999) revealed a strong Electrode Site by Epoch interaction at the midline sites

span.label: Behaviourally, masked visual primes speeded lexical decisions to both visual and auditory targets by roughly equal amounts, with no modality-by-repetition interaction.
span.quote: Simple effects ANOVAs revealed that the repetition effect was reliable for visual words (39ms effect, F(1,23) = 20.176, p < 0.001), and auditory words (40ms effect, F(1,23) = 14.957, p < 0.001), but no interaction between target modality and repetition (F(1,23) = 0.004, p < 0.947).

span.label: In the ERPs, within-modality repetition effects appeared early and spanned the N250 and N400, while cross-modal effects only emerged on the trailing edge of the N400 after the visual effect had ended.
span.quote: While the visual ERP repetition effects started early (200–300 ms) and continued through the traditional N400 epoch (300–500 ms), a comparable effect in the auditory modality was not significant until the offset phase of the typical N400 (550–750 ms), a time period by which the visual effect had completely dissipated.

span.label: Raising the prime duration from 50 ms to 67 ms made the cross-modal N400 priming effect both earlier and substantially larger.
span.quote: Our between-experiment analyses showed an earlier and much larger modulation of N400 amplitude in cross-modal repetition priming in Experiment 3 compared to Experiment 2.

span.label: The model's prediction that a longer prime would produce cross-modal effects in pre-N400 components was not supported: no N250 priming appeared for auditory targets even at 67 ms.
span.quote: However, contrary to this prediction we failed to find any evidence for standard priming effects (i.e., reduced negativity in the related condition) in early ERP components (i.e., the N250) with auditory targets at the longer prime duration of Experiment 3.

span.label: Within-modality (visual-visual) priming became smaller, not larger, as prime exposure increased from 50 to 67 ms.
span.quote: Within-modality repetition priming actually diminished with increasing prime exposure across Experiments 2 and 3.

span.label: At the short prime duration a small reversed (inverse) priming effect appeared in the cross-modal condition in the 200-300 ms window.
span.quote: One unpredicted result in Experiment 1 was a small inverse priming effect (repeated more negative than unrelated) in the cross-modal condition in the 200–300 ms measurement window over the right hemisphere.

span.label: N250 component
span.quote: Holcomb and Grainger referred to this as the N250 component and suggested that it reflects early sublexical processing in the visual word processing system.

span.label: N400 amplitude (as an index of semantic integration difficulty)
span.term: N400 amplitude (as an index of semantic integration difficulty)
span.quote: the most dominant view being that N400 amplitude is proportional to the difficulty of semantic integration

span.label: prime and target
span.quote: For both words and nonword pairs, the first member of each pair was referred to as the prime and the second member as the target .

span.label: masked priming variant (as a control on strategic processing)
span.term: masked priming variant (as a control on strategic processing)
span.quote: Compared to standard cross-modal priming, the masked priming variant has the advantage of preventing contamination from strategic factors that play a role a soon as participants become aware of the priming manipulation

span.label: repetition (repeated vs unrelated prime-target pair)
span.quote: In addition to the two levels of repetition (repeated/unrelated) and the two levels of word type (word/nonword), there was a third factor of target modality (visual and auditory) which resulted in four types of trials

span.label: target modality (visual vs auditory)
span.quote: Four separate repeated measures analyses of variance (ANOVAs) were conducted using the within-subject factors of repetition (repeated vs. unrelated) and modality (visual vs. auditory)

span.label: prime exposure duration (50 ms vs 67 ms)
span.term: prime exposure duration (50 ms vs 67 ms)
span.quote: Therefore, Experiment 3 was a direct replication of Experiment 2, the only change being that prime exposure duration was increased from 50 ms to 67 ms (i.e., from three vertical retrace intervals to four).

span.label: task (lexical decision vs go/no-go semantic categorization)
span.term: task (lexical decision vs go/no-go semantic categorization)
span.quote: In Experiment 1 subjects performed a lexical decision task.

span.label: ERP mean amplitude in four post-target latency windows
span.term: ERP mean amplitude in four post-target latency windows
span.quote: Mean amplitudes for four post-target onset latency windows were used to quantify the ERPs in this experiment: 0–150 ms, 200–300 ms, 300–500 ms, and 550–750 ms.

span.label: reaction time and percentage of errors
span.term: reaction time and percentage of errors
span.quote: The mean reaction times, percentage of errors, and standard error of the mean were calculated for each subject.

span.label: word length, frequency and form/semantic overlap of the pairs
span.term: word length, frequency and form/semantic overlap of the pairs
span.quote: Pairs of words were matched for length (four to six letters, average length 5.3 letters; auditory word stimuli: mean duration 640 ms, range 237–1007 ms) and frequency (between 10 and 431 per million;

span.label: counterbalanced stimulus lists across conditions
span.quote: Four counter-balanced lists were created so that across subjects, target words and nonwords appeared once in each of the four conditions.

span.label: 39ms / 40ms — size of the behavioural repetition priming effect for visual and auditory word targets in Experiment 1
span.quote: Simple effects ANOVAs revealed that the repetition effect was reliable for visual words (39ms effect, F(1,23) = 20.176, p < 0.001), and auditory words (40ms effect, F(1,23) = 14.957, p < 0.001), but no interaction between target modality and repetition (F(1,23) = 0.004, p < 0.947).

span.label: d' = 0.11 — prime visibility (sensitivity) in the Experiment 1 mask-effectiveness forced-choice test, not different from zero
span.quote: The average d’ value was 0.11, and this did not significantly differ from zero (t(23)=1.19, p =0.24).

span.label: 64% — proportion of masked primes correctly reported in the post-experiment visibility test with the longer 67 ms prime of Experiment 3
span.quote: In the post-ERP mask-effectiveness procedure participants correctly reported an average of 64% of primes.

span.label: 1.2 microvolt — amplitude of the late auditory (cross-modal) priming effect at Cz in Experiment 1
span.quote: it is worth noting that the current 1.2 microvolt auditory priming effect at Cz between 500 and 750 ms is relatively late and somewhat small compared to at least one previous cross-modal priming study

span.label: 50 ms to 67 ms — the single manipulated change in prime exposure duration between Experiments 2 and 3
span.quote: Therefore, Experiment 3 was a direct replication of Experiment 2, the only change being that prime exposure duration was increased from 50 ms to 67 ms (i.e., from three vertical retrace intervals to four).
